name: Temple filler

lead: Temple filler uses an injectable filler, usually hyaluronic acid, to fill the hollow at the side of the forehead that can appear with ageing or leanness. People use it for a smoother upper-face outline and better facial balance.

The filler adds volume deep in the temporal fossa, softening the concavity. It is a very common minimally invasive procedure, and much of the published literature is anatomical, including cadaver imaging, vessel mapping and ultrasound guidance studies on safer injection planes. Registered trials mostly treat the temple as one of several treated areas.

paras: A licensed clinician injects the temples in an office visit and the fill is visible on injection. People repeat treatments as the filler absorbs, and it is commonly done together with other facial areas.

The temple is a technically demanding site. Papers list contour irregularities, vascular occlusion, skin necrosis, hair loss, blindness, stroke and non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism, with blindness from retrograde embolization reported as rare but usually permanent. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.

angle.text: Temple filler fills the hollow at the side of the forehead, giving the upper face a smoother outline and better balance. Hyaluronic acid is placed deep in the temporal fossa to restore the lost volume. Most published research on the area is anatomical, focused on vessel mapping and safer injection planes.

lead: Temple filler is the injection of a dermal filler, most commonly hyaluronic acid (HA), into the temporal fossa to restore volume in temporal hollowing, a concavity at the side of the forehead that is associated with ageing and facial thinness. Practitioners describe it as improving facial balance and, by softening the hollow, giving the upper face a smoother outline.[1]

The temple is considered a technically demanding injection site. Papers describe temple volumisation as a very common minimally invasive facial procedure whose risks include contour irregularities, vascular occlusion, skin necrosis, hair loss, blindness, stroke and non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism.[1][2] A substantial share of the published literature on temple filler is anatomical: cadaver imaging, vessel mapping, ultrasound guidance and injection-plane techniques aimed at reducing vascular complications.[1][2][3][4][5]
Controlled clinical trials of filler specifically for the temple are limited; registered studies exist that include the temple among treated regions or combine it with other treatments.[6][7][8]

paras: Temple filler treats the hollowing of the temporal fossa, an area bounded by the forehead, brow and zygomatic arch. A paper on ultrasound-guided temple injection describes filler volumisation of the area as able to significantly improve facial balance and appearance, while noting its risks.[1]

The area contains vessels and nerves that complicate injection. A retrospective review of a previously undescribed accessory nerve and vessel running in the frontotemporal area discussed its implications for migraine surgery and cosmetic temple filler.[9] Cadaver studies using 3D CT of 56 heads injected with lead oxide mapped the temporal vessels to propose a more precise protocol for temple filler injection.[2]

Published technique papers describe several approaches to reduce risk. One group introduced ultrasound-guided HA injection targeting the interfascial space.[1] Another paper described a pinch-anatomy guide, noting that injectors often pinch or pull tissue with the non-dominant hand and that this deformation changes the relationship between tissue layers.[3] A further paper described a singular entry point technique for forehead and temple augmentation, from anatomical and clinical perspectives.[10]
A 2026 study used microvascular imaging to map temporal arteries for filler planning.[5] A commentary accompanied the ultrasound-guided technique paper.[11]

Most published work is anatomical or technique-focused rather than outcome trials.[1][2][3][5] Registered clinical studies that include the temple include a non-inferiority comparison of Art Filler Volume with Juvéderm Voluma on the midface, temple and jawline (NCT04645576, 98 participants, completed), a study of single-session microfocused ultrasound, botulinum toxin and temporal HA filler for non-surgical brow lifting (NCT07894822, 36 participants), and a comparison of poly-L-lactic acid injections in the temporal fossa versus the extended temporal fossa plus hairline (NCT06337747, 24 participants).[6][7][8] Other registered filler device studies cover facial volume in several areas (NCT04166292, NCT06872359), and a study of adipose-derived stem cells on fat-filler survival (NCT03965936) is also registered.[12][13][14]
No results from these registered studies were identified.
The risks listed in the ultrasound-guided technique paper include contour irregularities, vascular occlusion, skin necrosis, hair loss, blindness, stroke and non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism.[1]

A 2025 study investigated vascular anastomoses between the deep temporal and ophthalmic arteries to examine the pathway by which blindness could occur after temple injection, and later correspondence in the same journal commented on the work and received a reply.[4][15][16] Wikipedia notes that blindness from retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries is rare but usually permanent when it occurs.[17]
